 Ayo Dosunmu’s Stories Explain Chris Finch’s ‘Bad Blood’ Remark
 Janik Eckardt Updated 2026년 11월 7일 토 오후 10:16 UTC 0 IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Chris Finch sometimes wondered whether the Timberwolves’ offseason competition had gone too far. Ayo Dosunmu’s description of life inside the gym helps explain what the coach was hearing.
 In a November 5 letter for The Players’ Tribune , Dosunmu detailed the exchanges, challenges and increasingly ridiculous arguments that accompany Minnesota’s practices. Anthony Edwards features prominently, but Dosunmu makes clear that he eventually became a willing participant.
 “The energy in our gym is something you can’t even capture on video,” Dosunmu wrote . “They won’t allow it. It could get taken outta context the way we’re talking s*** and going so hard.”
 That account adds another perspective to Finch’s assessment after Minnesota’s October 23 win in Orlando. “That September gym, I thought at times there was a lot of kind of bad blood there,” Finch said . “There were a lot of times I thought it had boiled over.”
 Nov 6, 2026; New Orleans, Louisiana, USA; Minnesota Timberwolves guard Ayo Dosunmu (13) brings the ball up court against New Orleans Pelicans guard Jeremiah Fears (0) during the second half at Smoothie King Center. Mandatory Credit: Stephen Lew-Imagn Images Finch also emphasized that the players enjoyed the competition. Dosunmu’s stories show how that enjoyment can coexist with conversations that sound considerably less friendly from outside the group.
 His own introduction required some adjustment. After arriving from Chicago at last season’s trade deadline, Dosunmu initially concentrated on observing his new teammates and finding his place. He had spent his basketball life close to home, from growing up in Chicago to playing at Illinois and then for the Bulls.
 Minnesota presented a different environment. Edwards ensured it would be a loud one.
 Dosunmu described his teammate’s trash talk by invoking Kobe Bryant, Michael Jordan and Kevin Garnett before deciding Muhammad Ali might be the better comparison. Edwards, he wrote, would jog back after scoring while borrowing the boxer’s famous declarations about his own greatness.
 Eventually, Dosunmu stopped simply listening. “Once it gets to playoff time and the energy is a little different, I’m talking s*** back to Ant in practice, and I can see he’s going up a level,” he wrote.
 What followed was a running exchange of baskets and boasts. Edwards would score and declare himself too much to handle. Dosunmu would answer with a jumper and a response of his own. The argument eventually became so tangled that both players were trying to establish which one was “him,” losing track of their own declarations in the process.
 Dosunmu’s retelling is affectionate. He remembers the absurdity alongside the competition, giving readers a view of teammates pushing each other while enjoying the challenge.
 Advertisement
 That relationship also provides context for what he told reporters after the Orlando win.
 Oct 31, 2026; San Antonio, Texas, USA; Minnesota Timberwolves forward Joan Beringer (19) and guard Ayo Dosunmu (13) look over in the second half against the San Antonio Spurs at Frost Bank Center. Mandatory Credit: Daniel Dunn-Imagn Images “We were going at it for a month straight, competing,” Dosunmu said then . “No one wants to lose, everyone playing hard, making it hard on each other.”
 The earlier explanation concerned preparation: demanding workouts made regular-season physicality more manageable. His letter reveals the personalities behind that work and how he grew comfortable enough to contribute to it.
 The same willingness to challenge teammates extends beyond Edwards. After the Orlando game, Joan Beringer described Dosunmu as a big-brother figure who would tell him to “wake up” when his performance slipped.
 “I love this type of energy,” Beringer said .
 Those relationships make direct criticism easier to understand. Beringer welcomed the push because he believed Dosunmu was helping him. Dosunmu’s exchanges with Edwards similarly describe players responding to one another, with the basketball competition continuing underneath the talk.
 Edwards’ recovery from knee surgery has changed Minnesota’s lineup and increased Dosunmu’s responsibilities. In his letter, Dosunmu promised the team would maintain the energy its leading scorer helped establish.
 That gives the practice stories relevance beyond their entertainment value. The Wolves are trying to preserve a competitive standard while one of its most forceful voices is unavailable on the court. Finch heard sessions that sometimes sounded close to boiling over. Dosunmu remembers wanting to answer the next basket, deliver the next line and make Edwards raise his game again.
 His explanation of those exchanges ends with a sentiment that makes the tone unmistakable: “I love this team, man.”
